items.prompt: Define a cash flow forecast.
items.canonical_answer: A cash flow forecast is a financial plan that sets out the cash a business expects to receive and the cash it expects to pay out over a future period, normally month by month, together with the balance of cash it expects to hold at the end of each of those periods.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning only. The definition must carry the three elements: expected cash received, expected cash paid out, and the balance at the end of each future period. No example or evaluation required.

items.prompt: Define a cash outflow.
items.canonical_answer: A cash outflow is money actually paid out by the business in a period - payments to suppliers, wages and salaries, rent, insurance, electricity and water charges, interest, tax, repayment of borrowing, the purchase of equipment, and drawings or dividends. The test is that money leaves the bank account in that period, not that a cost was incurred in it.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning: money leaving the business in the period concerned.
Credit the definition rather than the list; one or two examples are sufficient illustration.
2 marks (AO1): a precise definition - money leaving the business in the period concerned; 1 mark for partial understanding.

items.prompt: Explain why a business prepares a cash flow forecast when it already prepares profit figures.
items.canonical_answer: Because the two answer different questions. Profit counts a sale when it is made and spreads the cost of equipment over the years it is used; a cash flow forecast counts a sale when the customer pays and shows the whole cost of the equipment in the period it leaves the bank. A business that is profitable over a period can therefore still be unable to meet its payments inside it. The forecast is built month by month so that the periods in which cash is expected to run short are visible in advance, which gives the business time to arrange finance or reschedule spending before the shortage arrives rather than after it.
marking_guidance: Reason: the purpose is to show the timing of cash, which a profit figure does not.
Must explain why the two differ - credit terms delaying receipts, and capital spending leaving in one lump.
Reward the consequence: advance warning gives time to act.

items.prompt: Explain the purpose a cash flow forecast serves when a business applies for finance.
items.canonical_answer: It answers the three questions the request turns on: when the money is needed, how much is needed, and when the business expects to be able to repay. A lender or investor assessing the risk is likely to ask to see one, because without it the timing of the need and of the repayment has to be taken on trust. A forecast showing a shortage of a known size, in known months, with the balance recovering afterwards, is a different proposition from an unsupported request for the same sum.
marking_guidance: Purpose: the forecast supplies the timing and size of the need and of the repayment.
The reason a lender values it must be given as a likelihood with a cause, not as a certainty about what a lender does.
Reward any two of: when needed, how much, when repayable.

items.prompt: Explain how preparing a cash flow forecast changes what a business is able to do about a cash shortage.
items.canonical_answer: The mechanism is time. The forecast converts a shortage that would otherwise be discovered on the day a payment falls due into a dated, quantified expectation several months ahead. Because the business knows the size and the month, it can negotiate an overdraft while it still has a choice of lender, reschedule a large payment before it is committed to, or bring receipts forward. The same shortage met without warning leaves only whatever can be arranged in days, and the terms available at that point tend to be worse. What the forecast does not do is explain why the shortage arises or remove it; it is a warning device, and the decisions that follow are a separate piece of work.
marking_guidance: Mechanism: advance warning widens the set of responses because arrangements take time to make.
The answer must say how the warning helps, not merely that it does.
Credit the boundary: the forecast warns, it does not diagnose or solve.

items.prompt: Kunene Blocks makes concrete blocks in Opuwo, sells on 30-day credit and is about to pay N$70 000 cash for a second mixer in February. Its owner says the business is profitable so a forecast is unnecessary. Explain why a cash flow forecast is still worth preparing for this business.
items.canonical_answer: Two facts in this business pull cash and profit apart. Selling on 30-day credit means January's sales are February's cash, so every month's receipts lag the month that earned them. The mixer is capital spending: it leaves the bank in full in February, while a profit calculation spreads its cost over the years the mixer is used. Both effects land in the same month, so February's payments can exceed February's receipts in a quarter the business trades profitably. Only a month-by-month forecast shows that, and it shows it before February, which is when an overdraft can still be arranged or the mixer purchase moved. The profit figure for the quarter reports the outcome and says nothing about February.
marking_guidance: Context: the answer must use the 30-day credit terms and the N$70 000 cash purchase, not general points about forecasts.
Reasoning: link each fact to the mechanism that separates cash from profit - receipts lag sales, capital spending leaves in one lump.
Conclusion: the forecast is worth preparing because it locates the month, in time to act.

items.prompt: Analyse the consequences for a building supplier of discovering a cash shortage in the week it arrives rather than three months in advance.
items.canonical_answer: Start from the condition: the shortage is the same size either way, and what differs is only the notice. With three months, the business can approach more than one lender, offer security, and present a forecast showing when the balance recovers, so it is negotiating. With a week, the only sources that can be arranged in days are an extension of the existing overdraft or a supplier's forbearance, and a business asking at that point is asking from weakness, so the rate and conditions it is offered are likely to be worse. If nothing can be arranged, payments are missed: suppliers put the account on hold, so materials stop arriving, and output falls just as the business most needs to trade its way out. Wages missed cost staff and reputation. The measurable consequence is a higher cost of finance at best and lost trading at worst, and the objective at risk is survival rather than profit - the business can be profitable and still fail here. The size of the effect depends on how large the gap is relative to the facilities already agreed; a shortage inside an existing overdraft limit produces none of this.
marking_guidance: Condition: the starting point is identical shortages differing only in notice given.
Mechanism: less time narrows the set of available sources and weakens the business's position, because arrangements take time to make.
Consequence: must reach a measurable result - higher cost of finance, or missed payments and lost output.
Objective or stakeholder: name survival, or suppliers and staff, as what is affected.
Credit the limiting condition: a gap within an agreed facility does not produce the chain.

items.prompt: Explain one limitation of a cash flow forecast that arises from the way its figures are produced.
items.canonical_answer: Every figure in it is an estimate, so the forecast is no more reliable than the assumptions behind it - how much will be sold, at what price, when customers actually pay, and what costs turn out to be. Because the closing balance of one period becomes the opening balance of the next, an error in one month is carried into every month after it, so a sales estimate that is out by a fifth leaves every later closing balance wrong. Reliability also falls with distance: next month's receipts can be estimated from orders already placed, while receipts eleven months out rest on sales nobody has yet made. That is why a forecast is normally rewritten as each month's actual figures come in.
marking_guidance: Limitation must be developed: estimates, therefore unreliable, therefore the balances built on them are unreliable too.
Credit the carry-forward: an error in one period leads to errors in all later periods.
Accept declining reliability with distance as the developed strand instead.

items.prompt: A learner writes: 'A business that is making a profit cannot run out of cash.' Correct the statement.
items.canonical_answer: The statement is wrong because profit and cash are measured differently. Profit counts a sale in the period it is made, whether or not the customer has paid; a cash flow forecast counts it in the period the money arrives. Profit also spreads the cost of a non-current asset across the years it is used, while the cash forecast shows the whole payment in the period it is made. A business selling on 60-day terms and buying equipment for cash can therefore be profitable over a quarter and be unable to meet its payments inside it. The corrected version: profit measures whether trading is worthwhile; the cash position measures whether the business can pay what falls due, and a business can be doing well on one and failing on the other.
marking_guidance: The error must be named: profit and cash are different measurements taken at different moments.
The correction must give at least one mechanism - credit terms, or capital spending.
Reward a corrected statement, not only a rejection of the original.

items.prompt: In March a Windhoek furniture shop sells N$60 000 of goods, all on 60-day credit, and receives no other money. Its costs for the month, all paid in March, are N$45 000. Explain the difference between the shop's net cash flow for March and the profit it earned in March.
items.canonical_answer: Net cash flow is the cash received in a month less the cash paid out in it; profit is the revenue of the month less its costs, whether or not the money has moved. For the shop, the N$60 000 of credit sales are March revenue but bring in no cash until May. So March shows a profit of N$15 000 and, in the same month, a net cash flow of minus N$45 000. The boundary is when the money moves against when the trade happens, which is why a negative net cash flow in March is not evidence that the shop made a loss.
marking_guidance: 1 mark (AO1): the difference identified - net cash flow counts money received and paid in the month, profit counts the trade of the month whether or not it has been paid for.

2 marks (AO2): applied to the shop - the N$60 000 of credit sales are March revenue but May cash, so March shows a profit of N$15 000 alongside a net cash flow of minus N$45 000; 1 mark for a generic contrast.
Boundary: when money moves against when trade happens; the two figures can differ in sign in the same month.

items.prompt: A forecast's closing balance row reads N$36 000, N$52 000, N$11 000, N$4 000 for four consecutive months. Explain what that row tells the business.
items.canonical_answer: Compared against each other, the four figures describe a direction rather than four separate states: the balance builds for two months and then falls in each of the last two, by N$41 000 and then by N$7 000. The business is not yet overdrawn, so nothing is due to be missed inside the four months. What the row means is that the fall began in month three and has not reversed, so on the direction shown the balance is close to turning negative in month five. Interpreting it means asking what changed in month three - a large payment, or a drop in receipts - because the answer decides whether the fall is a one-off step or a slope that continues.
marking_guidance: Comparison: the figures have to be read against each other and against zero, not one at a time.
Meaning: state the direction, the turning point and what it implies for the month after the forecast ends.
Interpretation must go beyond restating the four numbers.

items.prompt: Define the closing balance in a cash flow forecast.
items.canonical_answer: The closing balance is the amount of cash a business expects to hold at the end of a period. It is calculated as the opening balance plus the net cash flow of that period, and it becomes the opening balance of the next period. It is a currency amount, and a negative closing balance means the account is expected to be overdrawn.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning: cash expected at the end of the period.
Credit the definition; the formula and the carry-forward are acceptable supporting detail but the meaning must be there.

items.prompt: Okahandja Timber Supplies forecasts total cash inflows of N$145 000 and total cash outflows of N$134 000 for April. Its opening balance on 1 April is N$25 000. Calculate the net cash flow and the closing balance for April.
items.canonical_answer: Formula: net cash flow = total cash inflows - total cash outflows. Substituting: N$145 000 - N$134 000 = N$11 000. Formula: closing balance = opening balance + net cash flow. Substituting: N$25 000 + N$11 000 = N$36 000. Net cash flow for April is N$11 000 and the closing balance at 30 April is N$36 000. Interpretation: April's trading adds N$11 000 to the cash the business holds, so it ends the month with N$36 000 available and needs no overdraft in April.
marking_guidance: Formula: both relationships stated before substitution.
Substitution and working shown for each step.
Units: both answers in currency (N$), not as a number of units or a percentage.
Interpretation: one sentence saying what the closing balance means for the business - here, that April needs no borrowing.

items.prompt: A forecast shows a closing balance for August of N$4 000 and a net cash flow for August of minus N$21 000. Calculate the opening balance for August.
items.canonical_answer: Formula, rearranged from closing balance = opening balance + net cash flow: opening balance = closing balance - net cash flow. Substituting, and remembering that subtracting a negative net cash flow adds it back: N$4 000 + N$21 000 = N$25 000. The opening balance for August was N$25 000, in currency. Interpretation: the business started August with N$25 000 and spent all but N$4 000 of it during the month, so it enters September with almost no cushion against an unexpected payment.
marking_guidance: Formula: the rearranged relationship must be stated.
Substitution: the working must show the sign handled correctly - subtracting a negative adds.
Units: the answer is a currency amount.
Interpretation: say what the fall from N$25 000 to N$4 000 means for the business's position entering the next month.

items.prompt: A timber merchant's June column shows an opening balance of N$52 000, total cash outflows of N$310 000 and a closing balance of minus N$110 000. The inflow row has been left blank. Calculate total cash inflows for June.
items.canonical_answer: The balance fell from N$52 000 to minus N$110 000, a fall of N$162 000, so the net cash flow for June was minus N$162 000. Formula, rearranged: total cash inflows = net cash flow + total cash outflows. Substituting: N$310 000 - N$162 000 = N$148 000. Total cash inflows for June were N$148 000. Interpretation: the business still received N$148 000 of cash in June, so the shortfall is not caused by receipts drying up - it is caused by outflows of N$310 000 in a single month.

Substitution: working shown, with the negative net cash flow handled correctly.
Units: currency throughout.
Interpretation: what the recovered figure says about where the shortage comes from.

items.prompt: A merchant's June forecast shows inflows of N$148 000, outflows of N$310 000 and an opening balance of N$52 000; July shows inflows of N$128 000 and outflows of N$126 000. A customer due to pay N$40 000 in June now pays in July instead. Calculate the revised closing balances for June and July.
items.canonical_answer: June inflows fall to N$108 000 and July inflows rise to N$168 000; outflows are unchanged. June: outflows of N$310 000 against inflows of N$108 000 give a net outflow of N$202 000, so the revised June closing balance is N$52 000 less N$202 000, which is minus N$150 000. July: N$168 000 - N$126 000 = N$42 000 of net cash flow, added to an opening balance of minus N$150 000, gives a revised July closing balance of minus N$108 000. Both figures are currency amounts. Interpretation: June is N$40 000 worse and July's closing balance is exactly what it was before, because the payment moved between months inside the forecast rather than leaving it - the business's problem in June is deeper, and its position at the end of July is unchanged.
marking_guidance: Formula: net cash flow and closing balance relationships applied to both months.
Substitution: the amended inflow figures must be used and the June closing balance carried into July as its opening balance.
Units: currency, with the negative balances shown as negative.
Interpretation: the end-of-July balance is unchanged because the cash moved within the span; this is a statement of meaning, not an arithmetic check.

items.prompt: Identify, in order, the steps for completing one month's column of a cash flow forecast.
items.canonical_answer: Begin from what you are given: the opening balance for the month and the expected receipts and payments. First, add the receipts to get total cash inflows. Second, add the payments to get total cash outflows. Third, subtract outflows from inflows to get the net cash flow for that month, carrying the minus sign if outflows are larger. Fourth, add the net cash flow to the opening balance to get the closing balance. Finish by carrying that closing balance across as the opening balance of the next month, then repeat from the first step.
marking_guidance: Steps in the correct sequence; order is part of the answer.
Input: the answer must begin from the data given - opening balance, expected receipts, expected payments.
Each step stated as an action to carry out, not just named.
Result: the answer ends with the closing balance and its carry-forward to the next column.

items.prompt: A timber merchant with an agreed overdraft limit of N$40 000 forecasts closing balances of N$36 000 in April, N$52 000 in May, minus N$110 000 in June and minus N$108 000 in July. Explain what these figures mean for the business.

items.prompt: Explain how delaying a single payment by one month changes a cash flow forecast.
items.canonical_answer: Because the closing balance of one month is the opening balance of the next, a change in any month travels forward through every month after it. Delaying a payment removes it from the first month's outflows, so that month's net cash flow improves by the amount delayed and its closing balance rises by the same amount. That higher closing balance becomes the next month's opening balance, and the payment now appears in that month's outflows, so the second month's net cash flow worsens by the amount delayed. The two effects cancel: the closing balance at the end of the second month, and in every month after it, is exactly what it was before. Delay changes when cash leaves, not how much leaves, so it helps only where the problem is confined to the first month.
marking_guidance: Mechanism: the carry-forward of the closing balance is why one change moves later months.
The answer must show both halves - the first month better, the second worse by the same amount.
Credit the conclusion that the end-of-span balance is unchanged, and what that limits the method to.

items.prompt: A learner sees a negative net cash flow for March and concludes that the business made a loss in March. Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: Negative net cash flow means more cash left the business than entered it in March. A loss means costs exceeded revenue in March. They are different measurements and neither one implies the other. March can show negative net cash flow in a month of profitable trading if a large payment falls due in it - equipment bought for cash, a tax bill, a loan repayment - because none of those is a cost of March's trading, or not in full. March can equally show positive net cash flow in a month the business made a loss, if customers settled invoices from earlier months. The corrected reading: a negative net cash flow says the cash balance fell, and nothing more.
marking_guidance: The error must be named: a cash movement is being read as a trading result.
The correction must give a case where the two diverge, in at least one direction.
Reward the corrected statement of what negative net cash flow does mean.

items.prompt: Okahandja Timber Supplies planned to pay N$180 000 cash for a delivery vehicle in June, which left its June closing balance at minus N$110 000 against an overdraft limit of N$40 000. The supplier now offers three monthly payments of N$60 000 in June, July and August. Explain the effect of this change on the forecast.
items.canonical_answer: June's outflows fall by N$120 000, because only N$60 000 of the vehicle is paid then. June's net cash flow improves by that amount, so June's closing balance moves from minus N$110 000 to N$10 000 and the June breach of the N$40 000 facility disappears. That revised figure is July's opening balance, and July now carries an extra N$60 000 of outflows, so July runs a net outflow of N$58 000 and closes at minus N$48 000 - N$8 000 beyond the facility. The offer therefore shrinks the problem from a N$70 000 breach in June to an N$8 000 breach in July rather than removing it, which for this business is still worth having, because its ordinary trading generates cash every month and N$8 000 is a sum a temporary extension could reasonably cover. Two conditions attach. A third N$60 000 falls due in August, outside the four months shown, so the forecast has to be extended before the offer is accepted. And the supplier's price for paying in three parts has to be compared with the cost of borrowing the same sum.
marking_guidance: Context: the answer must use the N$180 000 purchase, the N$40 000 limit and the three-instalment offer.
Reasoning: show the mechanism - outflows fall in June, the revised closing balance carries into July, July takes an extra instalment.
Conclusion: the change shrinks the shortage and moves it into July rather than removing it, conditional on August being checked and the cost of the instalments being compared.
Do not credit an answer that treats June in isolation.

context.situation: amending a forecast after new information

items.prompt: Analyse what a forecast closing balance of minus N$110 000, against an agreed overdraft limit of N$40 000, means for a timber merchant in the month concerned.
items.canonical_answer: The starting point is that the balance is a forecast, not a fact, so what follows is conditional on the estimates holding. Given that they do, the business is forecast to need N$110 000 of borrowing at the end of that month and to have N$40 000 agreed, so N$70 000 of payments in that month has no funding behind it. The mechanism from there runs through what happens when a payment is presented and the account has no room: the bank may return it, so a supplier is unpaid, and a supplier that is unpaid can put the account on stop, which interrupts the timber supply the merchant sells. Wages unpaid have the same effect on staff. The measurable consequence is either an additional N$70 000 of finance arranged before that month, at whatever it costs, or interrupted trading in a month the business was otherwise selling normally. The objective at risk is survival: this is the point at which a profitable business fails. The whole chain is avoidable, which is the reason the forecast was prepared - the gap is known in advance and N$70 000 is a specific, arrangeable sum.

Mechanism: because the payments exceed the funding available, they cannot all be met, and an unpaid supplier or unpaid staff affect trading.
Consequence: reach the N$70 000 gap and one measurable effect of it.

items.prompt: A Swakopmund bakery starts June with minus N$20 000 in the bank. During June its receipts are N$8 000 more than its payments. Explain the difference between the bakery's opening balance for June and its net cash flow for June.
items.canonical_answer: The opening balance is a position at a moment: the cash the business holds at the start of the month, carried forward from everything before it. Net cash flow is a movement over the month: that month's inflows less its outflows. For the bakery the opening balance is minus N$20 000 and the net cash flow is N$8 000, so June is a good month that still ends overdrawn, with a closing balance of minus N$12 000. The difference is a stock against a flow, which is why a positive net cash flow does not by itself mean the business has cash.
marking_guidance: 1 mark (AO1): the difference identified - the opening balance is a position at the start of the month, net cash flow is the movement during it.
2 marks (AO2): applied to the bakery - a net cash flow of N$8 000 on an opening balance of minus N$20 000 still leaves June closing at minus N$12 000; 1 mark for a generic contrast.
Boundary: a position at a point in time against a movement over a period.

items.prompt: Explain how debt factoring improves a business's cash flow.
items.canonical_answer: The business sells its trade receivables - the amounts customers owe - to a factor. The factor advances most of the invoice value at once, commonly around 80 to 90 per cent, and collects from the customers itself. The mechanism is that cash which the forecast placed in a later period, when the customer was due to pay, is moved into the current one, so the current period's inflows rise and its closing balance rises with them. The factor keeps a fee, so the business receives less in total than it was owed, and the later period now receives nothing from those invoices. Which party bears the loss if a customer never pays depends on the agreement: under recourse factoring the business does, and under non-recourse factoring the factor does and prices the service higher accordingly.
marking_guidance: Mechanism: receivables are sold, so cash expected later arrives now.
The answer must say how the forecast changes - this period's inflows rise, the later period's fall.
Credit the cost: the fee means less is received than is owed.

items.prompt: Explain one benefit, to a business whose cash is tight, of leasing a machine rather than buying it outright.
items.canonical_answer: Buying outright puts the whole price into the outflows of one period, which is the single largest thing most forecasts contain and the commonest cause of a negative closing balance. Leasing replaces that with a series of smaller payments spread across the period of use, so the closing balance in the period the machine arrives is protected and the business obtains the capacity without needing the cash for it up front. The benefit is therefore developed through timing rather than cost: the total paid over the term normally exceeds the purchase price, so this buys a better cash profile and pays for it.
marking_guidance: Benefit must be developed: one large outflow becomes several small ones, so that period's closing balance is protected, which leads to the business obtaining the asset without the cash for it.
Credit an answer that acknowledges the total cost is usually higher, because that is what makes the benefit a trade-off rather than a free gain.

items.prompt: Explain one limitation of improving cash flow by taking longer to pay suppliers.
items.canonical_answer: It moves the payment rather than removing it, so the cash saved this period leaves in a later one and the closing balance at the end of the span is unchanged. The developed limitation is what it costs on the way: early-settlement discounts are given up, so the business pays more for the same goods; and the supplier relationship carries the strain. A supplier whose invoices are paid late may respond by shortening the terms it offers, asking for payment in advance, or refusing further credit, and any of those leaves the business worse off than before, because trade credit is itself a source of cash. Negotiating longer terms openly is a different act from paying late and tends to cost the relationship far less.
marking_guidance: Limitation must be developed, not listed: because the payment is only moved, the gain is temporary, and because the supplier is not consenting, the terms available later may worsen.
The supplier's reaction must be expressed as a likelihood, not a certainty.
Credit the distinction between negotiating longer terms and simply paying late.

items.prompt: Analyse the effect on cash flow of a wholesaler with monthly credit sales of N$200 000 reducing its customer credit period from 60 days to 30 days.
items.canonical_answer: Given that customers accept the new terms, the starting point is that the wholesaler is owed two months of sales at any moment and will be owed one. The mechanism is that each customer pays a month earlier than before, so during the month the change works through, the business receives that month's due receipts plus the month brought forward - a one-off improvement of about N$200 000 in the closing balance. After that, receipts settle back to one month's sales, N$200 000 a month, exactly as before. The measurable consequence is a permanent step up of roughly N$200 000 in the balance, not a higher rate of cash coming in. There is a counter-effect that can reverse it: customers value credit, and where competitors offer 60 days, some may take their orders elsewhere, so the business could end up collecting faster on a smaller volume of sales. The objective this serves is liquidity - surviving a known shortage - and it serves it well where the shortage is a one-off dip of N$200 000 or less, and poorly where the balance is falling period after period, because a one-off gain of that kind postpones a persistent problem rather than fixing it.
marking_guidance: Condition: the chain holds given customers accept the shorter terms.
Mechanism: because each payment arrives a month earlier, one month's receipts are pulled forward.
Consequence: the effect is a one-off gain of about N$200 000, not a rise in the monthly rate.
Objective or stakeholder: liquidity or survival, and the customers who may leave.
Reward the counter-effect and the condition that decides whether the method suits the shortage.

items.prompt: A wholesaler is owed N$200 000 by credit customers. A factor offers to advance 85 per cent of the invoice value immediately and charges a fee of 3 per cent of invoice value. Calculate the cash received immediately and the fee.
items.canonical_answer: Formula: advance = advance rate x invoice value; fee = fee rate x invoice value. Substituting: 0.85 x N$200 000 = N$170 000 received immediately, and 0.03 x N$200 000 = N$6 000 of fee. Both answers are currency amounts. items.prompt: A guesthouse in Swakopmund forecasts a shortfall of N$45 000 in May and June, its two quietest months, and expects strong bookings from July. It owns its building and had planned to refurbish six rooms in May at a cost of N$150 000. Explain which method of improving cash flow best fits this situation.
items.canonical_answer: The decisive facts are that the shortage is small relative to the planned refurbishment, that it lasts two months, and that trading recovers from July. Postponing the refurbishment removes the problem entirely and costs nothing in fees or interest, but the rooms are wanted for the July season, so postponing them may cost more in lost bookings than the shortfall itself. An agreed overdraft fits the shape of the need better: N$45 000 is small, the period is short and known, interest is charged on the amount actually drawn, and the July recovery repays it. Selling the building and renting it back would raise far more than is needed and would give up the asset permanently for a two-month problem. So the answer is an overdraft, with the refurbishment retimed only if the bank declines - and the reasoning that decides it is the match between the length of the shortage and the length of the finance.
marking_guidance: Context: the answer must use the N$45 000 size, the two-month length, the July recovery and the refurbishment.
Reasoning: link the shape of the shortage to the method, because a short known gap suits a flexible short facility.
Conclusion: reach a choice, with at least one rejected option and why it does not fit.
Do not credit a general list of methods applied to no facts.

items.prompt: A learner writes that a rise in sales improves a business's cash flow immediately. Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: A sale improves cash flow when the customer pays, not when the sale is made. Where a business sells on 60-day terms, extra sales in March are extra cash in May, while the materials, wages and delivery costs to supply them are paid in March. So a rise in sales can make the cash position worse in the short run, and the faster the growth the larger that effect - which is why growing businesses are a common case of cash shortage rather than an exception to it. The corrected statement: a rise in cash sales improves cash flow immediately; a rise in credit sales improves profit first and cash later, and costs cash in between.

items.prompt: Explain why most methods of improving cash flow do not help a business whose closing balance falls in every period.
items.canonical_answer: Because most of them move cash between periods rather than adding to the total the business generates. Chasing receivables, factoring, selling an idle asset and running down inventory each produce cash once, or pull forward cash that was arriving anyway; delaying a supplier payment postpones an outflow that still has to be made. Each therefore raises the balance by a fixed amount at a fixed moment. Where the balance is falling period after period, that one-off gain is consumed by the next period's deficit, so the business reaches the same position one period later - but with its receivables already sold, its suppliers already stretched and its idle assets already gone, so the same methods are no longer available. A falling balance in every period points to prices too low, costs too high or too little demand, and a change of timing leaves all three where they were.
marking_guidance: Limitation must be developed: because the methods shift cash rather than create it, the gain is finite, so a recurring deficit absorbs it.
Credit the second stage - the options are used up, leaving the business with fewer of them.
The answer must reach the conclusion that the cause lies in trading, not in timing.

items.prompt: A Windhoek printing firm sells entirely on 60-day credit and is owed N$400 000. It forecasts a shortfall of N$120 000 next month, caused by a tax payment, and positive balances thereafter. Evaluate whether it should use debt factoring to cover the shortfall.
items.canonical_answer: Judgement: on these facts the firm should not factor its receivables for this shortfall; an overdraft is the better instrument, with factoring held in reserve. The decisive criterion is the match between the shape of the need and the shape of the method. The need is one month long, N$120 000 in size, caused by a known dated payment, and followed by positive balances - that is precisely what an overdraft is built for, since interest runs only on what is drawn and the facility closes when the balance recovers. Factoring N$400 000 to cover N$120 000 would convert far more receivables than the gap requires and would leave the following months short of the receipts the forecast relies on to recover, so it risks turning a one-month problem into a two-month one. The strongest argument the other way is that factoring does not depend on the bank agreeing: if the firm has no facility and no security, an overdraft it cannot obtain is not an option, and a factor lending against N$400 000 of invoices may be easier to arrange. Factoring also transfers the collection work, which matters to a business whose customers all take 60 days. The condition that would reverse the judgement is therefore the availability and cost of the overdraft: if the bank declines, or prices it above the factor's fee, factoring becomes the right answer - and if it is used, the firm should factor only the invoices needed to cover N$120 000 and should establish whether the agreement is recourse or non-recourse, because that decides who carries the loss if a customer fails.
marking_guidance: Judgement: a clear recommendation, not a balanced list.
Context: the specific facts must drive it - N$120 000, one month, tax-driven, 60-day terms, N$400 000 owed.
Criterion: the decisive factor must be named as the match between the length and size of the need and the method.
Counterargument: the strongest case for factoring - it does not depend on the bank agreeing - must be addressed.
Condition: state what would reverse the judgement, such as the overdraft being refused or priced above the factoring fee.

context.situation: one-month shortfall caused by a dated payment

items.prompt: Explain how a cash flow forecast and the choice of a source of finance are connected.
items.canonical_answer: The forecast supplies the three facts the choice depends on. It gives the size of the shortage, which rules out sources too small to cover it and sources that would raise far more than is needed. It gives the length of the shortage, which is what the matching principle in 5.2 runs on: a gap lasting two months suits an overdraft, whose interest is charged on what is drawn, while a deficit running through the whole forecast needs finance with a term to match, or a change in the business. And it gives the point at which the balance recovers, which is the repayment date a lender is assessing. That is also why a lender considering a request is likely to ask for the forecast: without it the application states a sum without stating when it is needed or when it can be repaid. The judgement runs in one direction - the forecast constrains the choice of source, and the source chosen is then written back into the forecast as new inflows and the interest and repayments that follow it, which is how a business checks that the remedy is affordable.
marking_guidance: Reward the link across topics: the forecast produces size, length and recovery point, which are the inputs to the choice of source in 5.2.
The matching principle must appear, in substance if not by name.
The lender's interest must be expressed as a likelihood with a reason.
Credit the loop back: the chosen source changes the forecast.

items.prompt:
Namib Feeds (Pty) Ltd mills animal feed near Otjiwarongo and sells to commercial farmers on 30-day credit. Its cash balance on 1 July is N$60 000 and it has an agreed overdraft limit of N$50 000. Its forecast for the next four months is below, in N$.

| | Jul | Aug | Sep | Oct |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Total cash inflows | 340 000 | 310 000 | 290 000 | 360 000 |
| Total cash outflows | 305 000 | 330 000 | 470 000 | 315 000 |
| Net cash flow | 35 000 | ? | ? | 45 000 |
| Opening balance | 60 000 | 95 000 | ? | ? |
| Closing balance | 95 000 | ? | ? | ? |

September's outflows include N$160 000 for a new mill motor. (a) Calculate the missing net cash flow and closing balance figures for August, September and October. (b) Analyse what the completed row of closing balances tells the directors. (c) Evaluate whether Namib Feeds should postpone the motor or arrange additional finance for September.
items.canonical_answer:
(a) August: net cash flow = N$310 000 - N$330 000, a net outflow of N$20 000, so the closing balance is N$95 000 less N$20 000 = N$75 000. September: net cash flow = N$290 000 - N$470 000, a net outflow of N$180 000; opening balance N$75 000, so the closing balance is minus N$105 000. October: opening balance minus N$105 000, net cash flow N$45 000, so the closing balance is minus N$60 000.

(b) The row reads N$95 000, N$75 000, minus N$105 000, minus N$60 000. Against the N$50 000 facility, July and August are comfortable and September is N$55 000 beyond what the company can borrow. Read across, trading is sound: the only month in which outflows exceed inflows other than by the motor is August, and then by N$20 000. The motor alone accounts for N$160 000 of September's N$470 000. October recovers N$45 000, so the balance is still minus N$60 000 at the end of the forecast - the shortage does not clear itself inside the four months, and on October's rate it would take a further month or more to return to zero.

(c) Judgement: arrange finance rather than postpone the motor, provided the motor earns or protects more than the finance costs. The decisive criterion is what the motor is for. Milling capacity is the company's output: if the existing motor is failing, postponing it risks losing the October inflows the recovery depends on, and the cash saved is worth less than the trade lost. The shortage itself is well shaped for finance - N$55 000 beyond the facility, in one identified month, with positive net cash flow on either side - so an extended overdraft or a short-term facility matches it. The strongest argument for postponing is that it is certain and free: it removes the gap entirely without a fee, an interest charge or a lender's agreement, which matters if the bank may decline to extend the limit. The condition that decides it is therefore whether the motor can wait without interrupting milling, and whether the extension can be agreed before September. If the motor is a planned upgrade rather than a replacement, postponing is the better answer; if it is a replacement for a failing one, the finance is.
marking_guidance: (a) is marked on arithmetic: net cash flow and closing balance for each of the three months, each carried forward correctly, in currency.

(b) must compare the closing balances against the N$50 000 limit and against each other, identify the N$55 000 gap, and reach the meaning - trading is sound, one payment causes the problem, and it does not clear inside the forecast.
(c) judgement: a clear recommendation, not a list of both options.
(c) context: the facts of this business - the size of the gap, the single month, the October recovery, the purpose of the motor - must drive the answer.
(c) criterion: the decisive factor is what the motor does for output.
(c) counterargument: postponing is certain and free, and does not depend on the bank.
(c) condition: the answer must state what would reverse it, such as the motor being an upgrade rather than a replacement.

items.prompt: Kavango Crafts is a partnership making furniture in Rundu. Its forecast shows closing balances of N$18 000, minus N$26 000, minus N$41 000 and minus N$58 000 over four months, against an overdraft limit of N$30 000. Sales are steady and profitable. Customers, mostly retailers, take 60 days to pay; the partnership pays its timber suppliers in 30 days and holds three months of timber in store. Evaluate the best way for the partners to improve the partnership's cash flow position.
items.canonical_answer:
The shape of the problem decides the answer. The balance falls in every month by roughly N$15 000 to N$44 000, and the business is inside its facility only in the first month. This is a slope, not a dip, so a single one-off measure buys one month and leaves the partnership in the same position with fewer options.

Two facts in the case explain the slope. Receipts arrive 60 days after sale while timber is paid for in 30, so the partnership funds a 30-day gap on every order out of its own cash. And three months of timber in store is cash sitting as inventory rather than in the bank.

Recommendation, in order. First, reduce the timber held from three months to about one and a half. That releases roughly six weeks of purchases as a one-off improvement to the outflows over the next two months, and it costs nothing in fees - the risk is running short of a grade of timber, which is manageable where suppliers are local. Second, shorten the retailer credit period from 60 days to 30 on new orders, and chase the accounts already overdue. That pulls one month of receipts forward, a one-off gain, and the counter-effect is that a retailer offered 60 days elsewhere may take its orders there - so it is applied to the weakest accounts first, not across the board. Third, negotiate 45 or 60 days with the timber suppliers openly rather than simply paying late, which closes the remaining gap between paying and being paid without spending the relationship.

Those three change the timing. The decisive point is that they are not enough on their own if the underlying slope continues, because each produces cash once. So the fourth part of the recommendation is to check whether the deficit is genuinely a working-capital gap or a trading problem: sales are described as profitable, which points to the former, but the partners should confirm that the falling balance flattens once the three measures work through. The strongest argument against this whole approach is that it is slower than simply extending the overdraft, and a business facing an N$58 000 deficit against a N$30 000 limit may not have the months the measures need - so the immediate step is to ask the bank for a temporary extension to cover the transition, with the three measures as the reason the extension can be repaid. The recommendation reverses if the partnership cannot obtain that breathing space, in which case the credit-period change has to come first and be applied to every customer, accepting the risk to sales.
marking_guidance: 12 marks: AO1 2 (knowledge of the methods), AO2 2 (applied to Kavango Crafts' figures), AO3 2 (what each method does to the forecast), AO4 6 (a developed judgement in context that follows from the argument).
Judgement: a clear recommendation with an order of actions, not a list of methods.
Context: the answer must use the specific facts - 60-day receipts against 30-day payments, three months of inventory, the falling balances and the N$30 000 limit.
Criterion: the decisive factor is that the balance falls in every month, so one-off measures alone do not resolve it.
Counterargument: the measures take time to work, which an immediate deficit may not allow.
Condition: state what would change the recommendation, such as the bank refusing a temporary extension.
Each named method must be linked to its effect on the forecast, and the counter-effect of pressing customers must appear.

items.prompt: Plan an answer to: 'Preparing a cash flow forecast is the most useful thing a small business can do to avoid running out of cash.' Evaluate this view.
items.canonical_answer:
Define first: a cash flow forecast is a plan of expected receipts, expected payments and the resulting balance for each future period.

The case for the view. The forecast is the only document that dates a shortage before it arrives, and time is what converts a crisis into a negotiation - an overdraft arranged three months ahead is available on better terms than the same request made in the week wages are due. It is cheap: a small business can prepare one itself. It supports a request for finance, because a lender is likely to want the size, the timing and the repayment point, which are exactly what the table produces. And it lets a decision be tested before it is committed to.

The case against. Every figure is an estimate, so the forecast is no more reliable than the assumptions in it, and reliability falls the further ahead it reaches. It does not include the external events that most often cause shortages - a drought, a large customer failing. It identifies a shortage without explaining or correcting it: the methods in the third part of this topic do that work. And a business that prepares one and then does not act on it is no better placed than one that never prepared it.

Weigh rather than balance. The forecast is a necessary input to almost everything else a small business might do about cash - choosing a source of finance, deciding whether to shorten credit terms, deciding whether a purchase can be afforded - and none of those can be done well without it. That is a strong argument for its usefulness, and it is not the same as saying it is sufficient.

Judgement. Preparing the forecast is the right first action, because it is what makes every later action informed, but it is a diagnosis rather than a treatment. The decisive criterion is what the business does with it: a forecast acted on is the most useful single step; a forecast filed is worth nothing. The condition that would change the answer is the quality of the estimates - where a business has no order book and no trading history, the forecast's figures are close to guesses, and holding a cash reserve or arranging a facility in advance may protect it better than a table it cannot populate.
marking_guidance: Judgement: the plan must reach a decision on the view, not set out two sides and stop.
Context: the answer is about a small business, and the points must fit that - low cost to prepare, no finance department, thin trading history.
Criterion: the decisive factor must be named - whether the forecast is acted on.
Counterargument: the estimate problem and the fact that the forecast does not itself fix anything must be addressed, not mentioned.
Condition: state what would reverse the judgement, such as a start-up with no basis for its estimates.
Reward a plan that distinguishes necessary from sufficient.

items.prompt: A business lists the following for March: a credit sale of N$30 000 on 60-day terms, N$12 000 received from a customer who bought in January, wages of N$18 000 paid in March, and depreciation of N$4 000 on its delivery van. Identify which of these enter the March column of its cash flow forecast, and explain why.
items.canonical_answer: The N$12 000 received in March enters as a cash inflow, because the money arrives in March even though the sale was made in January. The N$18 000 of wages enters as a cash outflow, because it is paid in March. The N$30 000 credit sale does not enter the March column: on 60-day terms it becomes cash in May, and it is in May's column that it appears. The depreciation does not enter any column, because no money moves - it is a cost charged against profit, not a payment. The rule behind all four is the same: a cash flow forecast records movements of cash in the period they occur, not trade in the period it happens.
marking_guidance: Point: state, for each of the four, whether it enters the March column.
Reason: each decision must carry the reason - money moved in March, or it did not.
Context: the answer must handle each of the four items given, including depreciation, which enters no column at all.

items.prompt: Two friends opening a coffee shop in Windhoek have prepared profit projections showing a surplus in every month of their first year, and are about to ask a bank for N$250 000. Explain how preparing a cash flow forecast would change what they ask the bank for.
items.canonical_answer: The profit projection tells them the business works; it does not tell them when the money is needed. A forecast would show the fit-out and the first stock order leaving the bank before the shop opens, wages and rent falling due from day one, and takings building over the first months rather than arriving at their eventual level. The request would change in three ways as a result. The amount would be set by the deepest point of the forecast balance rather than by the cost of the fit-out. The timing would be specified, so they could ask for a facility that starts when it is needed and stops costing them when it is not. And the repayment point would be a month they can name, which is what a lender assessing the risk is likely to want to see. Without the forecast they are asking for a round sum with no dates attached.
marking_guidance: Context: the answer must use these facts - a start-up, no trading history, profit projections already made, a N$250 000 request.
Reasoning: link the forecast to each element of the request, because the size and timing of the need come from the balances.
Conclusion: reach a changed request - amount set by the deepest balance, dated, with a repayment point.

items.prompt: A farm supply shop built its forecast assuming customers pay 30 days after each sale. In practice they take 45 days. Explain what this does to the forecast.
items.canonical_answer: The error is in which column each receipt sits in, not in the total. Half of each month's credit sales now arrives a month later than the forecast placed it, so from the first affected month onwards each month's total cash inflows are understated by roughly half a month's credit sales - and every closing balance after it is overstated by that amount, because the shortfall carries forward. The shop is therefore planning against a cash position better than the one it will have, and the first month in which the forecast shows a small positive balance is a month in which it will actually be overdrawn. Correcting it means moving the affected receipts one column to the right and recalculating the net cash flow and every balance from that point on, not just adjusting the month in which the error was noticed.
marking_guidance: Context: the answer must use the 15-day slippage and the credit-sales share of receipts, not general remarks about inaccuracy.
Reasoning: the mechanism is that receipts move columns and the error carries forward through the balances.
Conclusion: the forecast overstates the cash position, and correcting it means recalculating from the affected month onward.

items.prompt: A bakery that opened four months ago, with no trading record and no assets beyond its ovens, forecasts a shortfall of N$15 000 in its third month of operation. Explain which methods of improving cash flow are genuinely open to it.
items.canonical_answer: Its position rules several methods out. It has no trade receivables worth factoring, because it sells for cash over the counter. It has no idle asset to sell, and selling the ovens would end the business. It has four months of history, so a bank assessing an overdraft request has little to assess and may decline or ask the owner for personal security. What is left acts on the outflows and on the owner. Suppliers can be asked for longer terms, though a business this new may not be offered credit at all. Ingredient stock can be run down, which is realistic for a bakery buying flour weekly and worth perhaps a few thousand dollars. Any planned equipment purchase can be postponed. And the most likely source is the owner: capital introduced from personal savings needs nobody's agreement and carries no interest, at the price of the owner's own money going into a business that may fail. So the realistic answer for a shortfall of this size is owner capital plus postponed spending, with a supplier negotiation attempted alongside.
marking_guidance: Context: the answer must use the age of the business, the absence of receivables and of spare assets, and the N$15 000 size.
Reasoning: each method must be ruled in or out because of a stated fact, not listed generically.
Conclusion: reach a specific combination that fits this business.

items.prompt: Evaluate how useful a twelve-month cash flow forecast is to a business that opened three months ago.
items.canonical_answer: Judgement: it is worth preparing, but its value is concentrated in the first three or four months and it should be rewritten monthly rather than relied on as a twelve-month plan. The decisive criterion is the quality of the estimates, because every figure in the table is one. For the next quarter this business has real information - orders placed, prices set, rent and wages known - so those columns are close to a plan. Months seven to twelve rest on sales volumes it has no history to estimate from, and the closing balance of month twelve carries every error made in the eleven before it, so the far end of the table is close to a guess presented as a figure. The strongest argument the other way is that a lender assessing a request for start-up finance is likely to want a full year, and that even poor estimates force the owners to state their assumptions where they can be argued with - a forecast that turns out wrong for a reason the owners can name is still worth more than no forecast. The condition that changes the answer is how the business uses it: rewritten each month as actual figures come in, the twelve-month horizon becomes a rolling plan and the objection largely falls away; filed in January and consulted in September, it is misleading precisely where the business is most exposed.
marking_guidance: Judgement: a clear verdict on usefulness, not a list of strengths and weaknesses.
Context: the answer must turn on this being a three-month-old business with no history.
Criterion: the decisive factor is the reliability of the estimates and how it decays with distance.
Counterargument: the lender's requirement, and the value of stating assumptions, must be addressed.
Condition: state what reverses it - rewriting the forecast monthly turns it into a rolling plan.

context.situation: new business planning a full year ahead
